name: The Riveters' Round
description:
No one knows who wrote 'The Riveters' Round' or when it first appeared — the earliest documented recording dates to 2187, captured on a handheld device by a labor journalist in a Tier 2 fabrication plant on GLMZ's southern industrial corridor, but workers interviewed at the time said they'd been singing it for years before that. The song is a true round — four overlapping vocal lines that can be sung by any number of people, designed to work in factory noise, in maintenance tunnels, in the rattling holds of cargo barges on the Lake Michigan freight lanes. The melody is built on a pentatonic scale with flatted sevenths that owes debts to both Appalachian shape-note singing and North Indian raga structures, and it requires no instruments, no amplification, no technology whatsoever.

The lyrics are functional and plain: they describe the sequence of a rivet-press operation in language that doubles as a meditation on the body's relationship to repetitive labor. 'Press and hold and breathe and turn / the metal knows what hands have earned.' It is sung at the start of shifts in some plants, at the end of shifts in others, and at funerals for workers in both Circuit and Shelf communities. Vantablack Media once attempted to register a copyright claim on a recorded version, which failed legally but generated enough ill will that the attempt is still cited as an example of corporate overreach in labor organizing materials.
creator: various
genre: work song, industrial folk round, unaccompanied vocal
audience: Tier 1 and 2 industrial workers, dock laborers, maintenance crews, cargo haulers, factory floor workers — anyone whose body is the primary instrument of their labor
cultural_impact: The Riveters' Round occupies a unique position in GLMZ's cultural memory as a song that has genuinely escaped ownership — it cannot be bought, suppressed, or co-opted because it exists only in the mouths of the people who sing it. Labor historians consider it the clearest surviving example of organic Shelf-Circuit cultural production, untouched by corporate mediation. When three hundred maintenance workers staged a sit-in at the GLMZ Central Cooling Authority in 2214, they sang it for eleven hours straight. The sound was audible three blocks away.
story_hooks: A Vantablack Media legal team has quietly resumed efforts to claim ownership of a specific recorded arrangement of The Riveters' Round — the player characters are hired by a labor collective to find and destroy every copy of that recording before the claim can be filed.

Deep in a sealed maintenance tunnel beneath GLMZ's oldest industrial district, someone has carved all four vocal lines of the round into the walls — and the carving dates to before the earliest known recording, suggesting the song is much older than anyone thought.

A Tier 4 composer has released an orchestral 'arrangement' of The Riveters' Round to significant critical acclaim on the Spire circuit — the Circuit and Shelf communities are furious, and someone has begun leaving threatening messages at the composer's studio.
